The Fat-tailed dunnart (Sminthopsis crassicaudata) is a small dasyurid marsupial inhabiting arid and semi-arid regions of southern Australia. Field studies employing mark-recapture techniques indicate that the maximum lifespan of this species is approximately 1825 days [am = approximately 1825 days] under the stable thermoregulatory conditions typical of its burrow microclimate, where core body temperature is maintained at 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C]. During the breeding season, females produce two distinct litters per year [F_R_i = two distinct litters per year], with each litter containing an average of seven pups [N_R_i = each litter containing an average of seven pups], a reproductive output that is relatively high compared to other small dasyurids. Neonates are altricial and remarkably diminutive at parturition, weighing a mere 0.01 grams [Wwb = 0.01 grams] at the moment of live birth. This extraordinarily low birth mass, among the smallest recorded for any terrestrial mammal, underscores the extreme altriciality of this marsupial and the reliance upon a brief intrauterine gestation followed by prolonged teat attachment and pouch development.

The gestation period of the Fat-tailed dunnart is notably brief, spanning only 14 days [tg = 14 days] at the species' typical maternal core temperature of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C]. This compressed gestation, characteristic of many dasyurid marsupials, reflects a reproductive strategy in which embryonic development is curtailed in utero and completed externally during an extended lactation phase. Following parturition, the altricial neonates migrate to the maternal pouch and attach permanently to a teat, entering a prolonged period of dependency. The time since birth at weaning is recorded as 69 days [tx = 69 days] under controlled laboratory conditions at a body temperature of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C], at which point the juveniles become nutritionally independent and begin consuming solid food items such as arthropods and small vertebrates. This weaning age is comparable to that of other small-bodied Sminthopsis species and is tightly linked to the seasonal abundance of invertebrate prey in the arid environment.

Juvenile Fat-tailed dunnarts continue to grow rapidly after weaning, undergoing substantial somatic development before reaching reproductive competence. Attainment of puberty, defined by the onset of gametogenesis and the first detectable signs of gonadal activity, occurs at 115 days since birth [tp = 115 days since birth] when individuals are maintained at a thermoneutral body temperature of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C]. This developmental milestone marks a critical transition from the non-reproductive juvenile stage to the reproductively viable subadult phase. The timing of puberty in this species is influenced by a combination of photoperiod, nutritional condition, and the attainment of a sufficient adult body mass. The ultimate wet weight attained by fully grown adults in the wild averages 15 grams [Wwi = 15 grams], a modest size that positions Sminthopsis crassicaudata among the intermediate-sized members of its genus. This adult body mass is consistent across most of its geographic range, though slight variations may occur depending on local rainfall patterns and prey density.

Comparative physiological studies highlight several life-history trade-offs associated with the small body size and arid-zone lifestyle of this dasyurid. The adult body mass of approximately 15 grams [Wwi = approximately 15 grams] imposes constraints on thermoregulation, water conservation, and energy allocation during reproduction. Under the warm thermal conditions typical of the species' burrow environment, where core body temperature stabilises at 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C], the maximum recorded lifespan extends to around 1825 days [am = around 1825 days], a duration that is relatively long for a mammal of this size. This longevity is facilitated by the species' ability to enter facultative torpor during periods of food scarcity, thereby conserving metabolic resources. The combination of a brief gestation period of just 14 days [tg = 14 days] and a relatively extended overall lifespan suggests a life-history strategy that balances rapid reproduction against sustained survival in a variable environment at a temperature of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C].

Ecologically, the Fat-tailed dunnart occupies a niche characterised by extreme temperature fluctuations and sporadic resource availability, which has shaped its distinctive life-history traits. The capacity to delay puberty until 115 days since birth [tp = 115 days since birth] provides young individuals with an extended period of somatic growth before investing in reproduction, a critical feature in an environment where body condition strongly predicts breeding success at a temperature of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C]. The weaning age of 69 days since birth [tx = 69 days since birth] coincides with the peak abundance of crickets and spiders in late spring, ensuring that newly independent juveniles have access to abundant prey at a temperature of 35.2 °C [T = 35.2 °C]. Field observations confirm that females produce a maximum of two litters per year [F_R_i = two litters per year] with seven pups per litter [N_R_i = seven pups per litter], a conservative reproductive strategy that balances offspring number against the energetic demands of lactation in a resource-poor habitat. The species' low birth mass of 0.01 grams [Wwb = 0.01 grams] and rapid development to an ultimate mass of 15 grams [Wwi = 15 grams] exemplify the extreme altriciality characteristic of dasyurid marsupials, reflecting an evolutionary compromise between gestational efficiency and postnatal maternal investment.
